newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian PM leads more crisis talks as West warns.
newsitem.headline: Albanian PM leads more crisis talks as West warns.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino led more efforts on Monday to resolve a crisis over planned elections as Western governments kept up the pressure for a compromise.

"We will try to decide something with the parties today," Fino said during a short break in talks with the other parties of his national unity government, most of which have threatened to boycott the June 29 vote.

The elections are seen as vital to stop Albania slipping back into the unrest of February and March, when people left penniless by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes took to the streets in an orgy of looting and riots.
The threatened boycott is over disputed election rules, which opponents say favour President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel kept up constant Western pressure for a compromise as he spoke with Fino by telephone late on Sunday.
"This is in the interests of the Albanians and of the international community, which is committed to help Albania overcome the crisis," state-run news agency ATA quoted Kinkel as telling Fino.
An official of the Socialist Party, one of those opposed to the election law, said parties were compiling a final draft of demanded amendments and would hand it to Berisha.
Under the constitution, Berisha can amend the election law by decree, without recalling parliament, politicians say.
"The government is working to formalise the proposals of the parties and introduce them to the president after the government considers them in general," the official said.
"All efforts will be made so that changes are made which guarantee a normal electoral process," he added.
Fino leads the nine-party Government of National Reconciliation, which Berisha was forced to install in March to calm the population as the rioting reached a peak.
The right-wing Democratic Party is also a member of the government and was present at the talks which Fino, a Socialist, was holding.
Kinkel's warning was the latest of a series of statements from Western governments urging compromise.
The European Union, Italy and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) have said they may withdraw aid unless free and fair elections go ahead.
Italy, which leads a multinational troop force protecting aid supplies and providing the only semblance of order in some areas, has said it may pull out if the elections fail.
Parties opposed to the election law want responsibility for administering the polls to be transferred from the president to the unity government.
Besides the right for the government to name the electoral commission, they seek changes in voting districts and a legal definition of the status of international monitors.

They also want the head of the secret police and the head of the radio and television council, which controls the only national TV channel, to be named within three days, and to make sure both bodies are neutral in the election.
In the last elections in 1996, the Socialists pulled out on the last day. The international community wants to avoid a repeat of that poll, which the OSCE described as deeply flawed.
